lesson.title: Are These Strings Equal? Comparing Text with Operators
lesson.summary: Strings support ==, <, >, and the other comparison operators from Comparison Operators, using case-sensitive, character-by-character lexicographic order.
lesson.body:
Strings support the same comparison operators you learned in Comparison Operators, ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >=, but applying them to text rather than numbers means understanding how Python decides that one string is "greater than" or "less than" another. This chapter builds directly on String Basics, since comparison depends on knowing that a string is a sequence of individual characters, each of which has an underlying numeric code.

Equality is the simplest case: "cat" == "cat" is True only if every character matches in the same position, so "cat" == "Cat" is False, since lowercase 'c' and uppercase 'C' are different characters as far as Python is concerned, even though they represent the same letter to a human. This is the exact same case-sensitivity issue that motivated the Upper and Lower Methods chapter: normalizing both sides with .lower() before comparing, "cat".lower() == "Cat".lower(), sidesteps the problem entirely.

Ordering comparisons like < and > use what is called lexicographic order, essentially dictionary order, comparing strings character by character from the left until a difference is found. Trace "apple" < "banana": Python compares the first characters, 'a' versus 'b'. Since 'a' comes before 'b' in the underlying character ordering, the comparison stops immediately and returns True, without even looking at the rest of either string. Now trace "apple" < "apply": the first three characters, 'a', 'p', 'p', match exactly, so Python moves to the fourth character, 'l' versus 'l', which also matches, then the fifth character, 'e' versus 'y'. Since 'e' comes before 'y', the result is True. Longer shared prefixes just mean the comparison looks further before finding the deciding character.

Case matters here too, in a way that surprises people. All uppercase letters come before all lowercase letters in Python's character ordering, so "Zebra" < "apple" is actually True, because uppercase 'Z' has a smaller underlying code than lowercase 'a'. This is why sorting a mixed-case list of words with plain < comparisons, or the built-in sorted() function, groups all the capitalized words before all the lowercase ones rather than blending them the way a dictionary would. If you want a comparison that matches human alphabetical expectations, normalize case first: compare word1.lower() < word2.lower() instead of comparing the raw strings.

A concrete example: sorting a list of names for a class roster.

names = ["zoe", "Amir", "beth"]
names.sort(key=str.lower)
print(names)  # ["Amir", "beth", "zoe"]

Passing key=str.lower tells .sort() to compare a lowercase version of each name when deciding order, while leaving the original capitalization in the final list untouched. Without that key, mixing cases like "amir" and "Beth" into the list would produce a strange, non-alphabetical-looking order, since the raw comparison would sort by character code rather than by letter.
